CausalChain: DDR gene alterations -> Accumulation of cytosolic DNA fragments -> Activation of cGAS-STING pathway -> Production of type I interferons (immune activation) -> High TGF-β levels suppress interferon signaling and T-cell infiltration -> TGF-β blockade removes suppression -> Combined DDR modulation and TGF-β inhibition leads to enhanced T cell-mediated antitumor response -> Improved efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancer, precision-guided dual modulation of the DDR and TGF-β pathways—achieved via state-of-the-art genomic profiling, targeted drug delivery systems, and digital monitoring of immune biomarkers—will activate the cGAS-STING-mediated innate immune response while alleviating TGF-β-induced immunosuppression. This combinatorial approach is expected to transform the tumor microenvironment from ‘cold’ to ‘hot’ by leveraging DDR inhibition to accumulate cytosolic DNA fragments and activate type I interferon pathways, and by concurrently blocking TGF-β to enable robust T-cell infiltration. The resultant enhancement in immune activation is predicted to synergize with immune checkpoint inhibitors, thereby improving therapeutic outcomes in BTC.
Abstract: Biliary tract cancer (BTC) presents a formidable therapeutic challenge due to its aggressive, heterogeneous nature and its predominately ‘cold’ tumor microenvironment that limits the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Here, we propose a precision medicine approach that leverages contemporary genomic profiling, advanced drug delivery systems, and real‐time biomarker monitoring to co-target the DNA damage response (DDR) and TGF‐β signaling pathways. Inhibiting DDR is hypothesized to trigger the cGAS-STING pathway through the accumulation of cytosolic DNA fragments, thereby enhancing type I interferon production and innate immune activation. Concurrently, TGF-β inhibition is expected to alleviate immunosuppression, further promoting T-cell infiltration. This dual strategy is designed to reliably convert the tumor microenvironment from ‘cold’ to ‘hot,’ ultimately synergizing with ICIs to improve clinical outcomes in BTC patients.
Orignal_vs_New: The new hypothesis expands upon the original by incorporating contemporary technological capabilities and a more refined implementation strategy. It retains the original causal chain: DDR gene alterations leading to cytosolic DNA accumulation, cGAS-STING activation, and subsequent type I interferon production, which is suppressed by TGF-β in the tumor microenvironment. The revised version explicitly integrates modern precision medicine tools, such as advanced genomic profiling, targeted drug delivery, and digital biomarker monitoring, to tailor DDR modulation and TGF-β inhibition in a controlled manner. This update addresses the observed heterogeneity in BTC and the need for optimized dosing, timing, and patient selection, thereby enhancing both the scientific rationale and practical applicability of the hypothesis.
